02 / Learning & classification

Three milestones, one learning problem

Fitting a line, estimating a class probability and training a neural network all require parameters to be learned from observations.

The central question: which parameters explain the observations and predict new cases well?

1805 · LegendreLeast squares: combine noisy observations by minimising squared errors.
1958 · CoxBinary regression: model how the probability of 1 depends on predictors.
1986 · Rumelhart, Hinton & WilliamsBackpropagation: organise the chain rule across multilayer networks.
Model → objective function → optimisation → prediction.

Training is a loop; inference is an evaluation

InitialiseChoose parameters, a loss, a learning rate and a stopping rule.
Predict and scoreCompute predictions and mean training loss.
Differentiate and updateCompute all gradients, then update the parameters.
RepeatStop using the predefined rule; keep the resulting parameters.

At inference, keep parameters fixed and evaluate the learned function on a new input.

02 / Generalisation

Three datasets, three distinct questions

Low training loss describes cases already used to fit the model. Our goal concerns future cases.

Split before fitting. The split should reflect deployment: future dates or new users may require temporal or grouped splits.

Repeatedly inspecting test results turns the test set into another source of selection.

Training · fitEstimate model parameters using the training loss.
Validation · selectChoose complexity, hyperparameters and decision threshold.
Test · reportAfter choices are frozen, estimate performance on untouched examples.
Generalisation is measured on data that did not guide fitting or selection.

02 / Classification: probability model

Classification predicts categories

A classification target is a category. Its numerical code identifies a class; it does not represent a measured quantity.

BinaryTwo mutually exclusive outcomes: spam or legitimate email.
MulticlassOne of several classes: the digit 0, 1, …, 9.
MultilabelSeveral labels may apply: a photo can contain both a person and a bicycle.

Learn a binary probability model, convert its output into a class decision, then evaluate the decisions.

Logistic regression is a classification model despite the word “regression” in its name.

Task → probability model → class decision → classification evaluation.

02 / Classification: decisions & metrics

Accuracy: how many decisions are correct?

Count every correct decision, positive or negative, and divide by the total number of cases.

This measure gives equal weight to every correctly or incorrectly classified case.

Our eight cases: 6 correct decisions and 2 errors. The two errors have different practical meanings.

Accuracy describes overall correctness but does not distinguish false alerts from missed events.
Ting Tan · EEEA · Oct 2026 · R5, R730 / 53
02 / Classification: decisions & metrics

Precision and recall use different denominators

Precision: when the classifier raises an alert, how often is it right?

The predicted-positive group is A, B, C, D. Three of these four alerts are correct.

False positives reduce precision. This matters when reviewing an alert consumes time or resources.

Recall: among the events that really occurred, how many were detected?

The actual-positive group is A, B, D, E. Three of these four events were detected.

False negatives reduce recall. Recall is also called sensitivity or true positive rate (TPR).

Precision starts with predictions; recall starts with observed positives.
Ting Tan · EEEA · Oct 2026 · R5, R731 / 53
02 / Classification: decisions & metrics

F1 combines precision and recall; specificity checks negatives

F1 is the harmonic mean of precision P and recall R. It is high only when both are high.

F1 ignores true negatives. It summarises two rates, but does not replace an application-specific cost analysis.

Specificity measures how many actual negatives are correctly left unflagged.

Here specificity = 0.75 and FPR = 0.25. Undefined denominators require an explicitly reported convention.

Recall uses actual positives; specificity and FPR use actual negatives.

02 / Classification: decisions & metrics

ROC–AUC evaluates ranking across thresholds

Lower the threshold from above every score to below every score. At each step, count TP and FP and plot one point.

ROC plots TPR vertically against FPR horizontally. A strong classifier approaches the upper-left corner.

Area under the ROC curve: AUC = 0.875 here. A random ranking has expected AUC 0.5; a perfect ranking has AUC 1.

Same eight cases. At : (FPR, TPR) = (0, 0.5). At : (0.25, 0.75).

AUC summarises ranking; it does not choose a deployment threshold or assess probability calibration.

02 / Classification: decisions & metrics

The PR curve focuses on positive predictions

Sweep the same thresholds, now plotting precision vertically against recall horizontally.

PR directly shows how reliable alerts remain as more actual positives are detected. It is especially informative when positives are rare.

Average precision (AP) weights precision by the gain in recall. Here AP = 0.8875. This uses a step-based convention, not trapezoidal PR area.

Same cases; positive fraction = 4/8 = 0.5. Points are linked in threshold order. The zero-alert endpoint uses precision = 1 for plotting.

Precision depends on class prevalence: compare PR results on comparable populations.

02 / Additional concepts

A14 · Extend evaluation to multiple classes

For mutually exclusive classes, use a K × K confusion matrix. To compute class-k precision, recall and F1, treat k as positive and all other classes as negative.

Macro gives each class equal weight. Weighted averaging uses class counts and can be dominated by common classes.

MicroPool TP, FP and FN over classes, then compute the metric.
Single-label special caseOver all classes, micro-precision = micro-recall = micro-F1 = accuracy, provided each case receives exactly one predicted label.
MultilabelSeveral labels can be true for one case. Specify label-wise versus sample-wise averaging; the single-label identity no longer generally holds.
For multiclass results, state which classes and averaging convention were used.
